KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Surface low pressure will track roughly along or just south of
the St. Lawrence River Valley and drag a strong cold front
through New England this evening into tonight. Out ahead of the
front, it's currently pretty dreary out in most places with 
overcast skies and fog, rain and drizzle. Temperatures have 
started to trend up slowly as southerly flow increases, and a 
warm front has made its way into southern NH, where temperatures
have warmed into the lower 60s of 2pm. 

The steadier rain is currently north across central and 
northern portions of the area, but looking upstream, more
showers are on the way for later this afternoon and early 
evening as the cold front approaches. CAMS are showing a couple 
hundred J/kg of MUCAPE that may be sufficient for a couple of 
thunderstorms across the southern half of NH and into far 
southwest ME. Chances appear low, but if any storm that 
develops can become surface-based, there is enough wind shear 
for strong wind gusts. The better chance of this occurring is 
across southern NH, which SPC has placed in a Marginal Risk 
(level 1/5) of severe weather. Showers are expected to end from
west to east this evening, and roughly another 0.10" of 0.25"
precipitation between now and then.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Northwest winds become breezy behind the front late this 
evening and continue through tonight with gusts of 25 to 35 mph.
Based on hi-res guidance, these breezy conditions should kick in
late evening to around midnight. These winds will carry in a 
much colder airmass, and upslope mountains rain showers are 
expected to transition to snow showers overnight, which should 
continue into at least the first part of Saturday. Increasing 
Froude numbers tonight/early Saturday could result in some 
clouds and possibly a couple of rain or snow showers spilling 
over downwind of the mountains if we can hold onto enough low 
level moisture. The combination of temperatures falling into the
30s to low 40s and gusty winds will make for wind chills in the
20s and 30s toward daybreak Saturday, possibly teens across the
north.

Cold air advection continues into Saturday, making it feel rather 
blustery out. Temperatures only recover somewhat into the 40s south 
of the mountains, but breezy NW winds of 25-35 mph will keep wind 
chills mostly in the 30s. Across the north, winds chills are 
expected to stay below freezing through the day. One silver lining 
is that a push of drier air will bring mostly sunny skies downwind 
of the mountains by the afternoon while diminishing clouds/upslope 
precip in the mountains.  

For hikers: Conditions will be dangerous and wintry in the higher 
terrain. In addition to snow showers, winds will be much higher
and and temperatures much colder, making for winds chills in 
the single digits to possibly below zero above tree line. 

Winds will diminish Saturday night as high pressure builds overhead, 
bringing favorable conditions for radiational cooling. I've gone a 
cooler than the NBM on low temperatures with most of the area seeing 
lows in the 20s and possibly teens in the the northern valleys. 

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
High pressure crests overhead on Sunday which should allow for 
a warmer feeling day as winds calm. Under full sun we should be 
able to mix into the low 50s south of the mountains, and into 
the mid to upper 40s to the north. Clear and calm conditions 
continue into Sunday night setting up for strong radiational 
cooling. I have gone ahead and already started to capture that 
trend by blending colder MOS guidance into the NBM. The result 
is widespread temperatures in the 20s with only the immediate 
coast hovering near or above freezing.

The center of the high pressure moves off to the east Monday 
but for the most part should stay nosed in for the better the 
part of the day resulting in mostly clear skies and afternoon 
temperatures mixing into the mid to upper 50s for the majority 
of the area. At the same time low pressure develops off the 
coast of the Carolinas where it looks like it is going to 
meander into midweek. It may meander just far enough north 
Monday night to spread some high and mid-level clouds into the 
coastal plain and potentially up to the foothills. If it is just
mostly high clouds we could see another night with decent 
radiational cooling, but if the trend continues to bring it 
further north and more midlevel clouds make it as well it will 
remain warmer. As a result we will roll with NBM for now which 
is a smattering of upper 20s to low 30s for much of the area, 
and upper 30s in southeastern New Hampshire.

High pressure begins to push low pressure back to the south 
during the day Tuesday which is going to bring about clearing 
skies, and probably the warmest day of the week with widespread 
low 60s. Seasonable temperatures and dry conditions then
